title: A comparison on constrain encoding methods for quantum approximate optimization algorithm
abstract_summary: This preprint numerically compares three methods for encoding linear constraints into QAOA—quadratization (QUBO), penalty dephasing, and the quantum Zeno effect—using the knapsack problem as a case study. The study reports trade-offs: QUBO uses fewer qubits and two-qubit gates but yields a more complex optimization landscape and longer classical optimization, penalty dephasing improves solution probability with more layers at the cost of extra resources, and the Zeno approach is theoretically promising but incurs runtime overheads from frequent mid-circuit measurements.
methodology_description: The authors performed a numerical, simulation-based comparison of three methods to encode linear constraints into QAOA for the 0/1 knapsack problem: (1) quadratization to a QUBO (penalty embedding into the cost Hamiltonian), (2) penalty dephasing (explicit constraint testing via an adder + flag qubit and applying a controlled phase penalty to infeasible branches), and (3) constraint enforcement via the quantum Zeno effect (frequent mid-circuit measurements of a flag qubit that indicates constraint violation, without post-selection). For all methods the first m qubits encode decision bits x_i, ancilla qubits encode weights/sums (c = ceil(log2(W)) + 1), and the mixing Hamiltonian is a Pauli-X array on the data register (and on ancilla in the QUBO case when required). Circuits use Hadamard initialization, alternating unitary layers U(H_C, gamma) and U(H_B, beta) to form a p-layer QAOA ansatz, and classical optimization of parameters (gamma, beta) using the COBYLA optimizer from scipy. The weight adder is implemented by a QFT-based adder. For the QUBO approach they introduce slack variables to make weight range a power of two and map binary variables x_i to (I + Z)/2 to build an Ising Hamiltonian; penalty multiplier P = 10 was used in reported experiments. For penalty dephasing a flag qubit is set by testing the computed weight against W and infeasible branches receive a controlled phase with penalty strength alpha = 10000. For Zeno, the ADD and TEST subroutines are used but the flag qubit is measured repeatedly and reinitialized to |0> (no post-selection). Experiments are classical simulations run on commercial laptops, averaging results over 50 randomly generated knapsack instances; problem sizes and QAOA depth p were varied (examples include sizes m in {3,4,5,6} and p in {1,3,5,7}) and metrics recorded include resource usage (ancilla qubits, two-qubit gates per layer) and performance metrics (probability of best feasible solution, feasibility ratio, and normalized average performance).

dataset_used: Randomly generated combinatorial knapsack problem instances (0/1 knapsack). Each instance has m items with integer weights w_i and values v_i, and capacity W. Instances were generated randomly; experiments averaged over 50 instances for each configuration.

experiment_input.sizes_evaluated: m (number of items) varied; examples shown for m in {3,4,5,6}; some experiments fixed m=5
experiment_input.preprocessing: Values v_i normalized when encoded as phase; slack variable added to transform capacity W into a power-of-two bound when using QUBO (so c = ceil(log2(W)) + 1 ancilla qubits); binary decomposition of weight sums into ancilla qubits via QFT adder.

high_level_pipeline: Generate 50 random knapsack instances for each (m,W) configuration.
For each instance and for each encoding method (QUBO, penalty dephasing, Zeno):
1) Map decision bits x_i to qubits (first m qubits).

2) Build circuit-specific subroutines: QUBO -> build Ising H_C including penalty (P=10) and extend qubit register by c ancillas; Penalty dephasing -> ADD (QFT adder) to compute Weight(x) into ancilla, TEST to set a flag qubit, controlled phase PENAL (alpha=10000) on data qubits conditioned on flag, REINIT by uncomputing ADD; Zeno -> ADD + TEST, measure flag qubit each layer and reprepare |0>, do not post-select.
3) Initialize state with Hadamards, then apply p layers of alternating U(H_C, gamma) and U(H_B, beta) (mixing H_B = Pauli-X array on data register; in QUBO H_B acts on data+ancilla as required).
4) Use COBYLA (scipy) to optimize parameters (gamma, beta) to minimize expected cost ⟨H_C⟩; record number of classical optimizer iterations to convergence.
5) Measure final state (sampling implied by simulation) to obtain solution probabilities and compute performance metrics.
Aggregate metrics across 50 instances and report averages and interquartile ranges.

experiment_process.notes: Zeno experiments used mid-circuit measurements and reinitialization without post-selection; QFT-based adder used for weight summation.

key_findings: [supported] In classical simulations on random knapsack instances, quadratization (QUBO) required fewer ancilla qubits and fewer two‑qubit gates per QAOA layer than both penalty dephasing and the quantum Zeno approach.

[supported] Under the tested settings (simulations averaged over 50 random instances), the QUBO encoding required more classical optimization iterations and had a longer total classical simulation runtime than the other two methods.

[supported] Penalty dephasing increased the probability of finding the best feasible solution as the number of QAOA layers increased and exhibited the best average performance at p = 5 in the reported experiments.

[supported] The quantum Zeno encoding produced longer wall‑clock simulation runtimes despite often needing fewer optimizer iterations; the authors observed this increased cost when simulating mid‑circuit measurements (mixed states).
[supported] For all three encodings, ancilla qubit counts and two‑qubit gate counts per layer increased with problem size.

[supported] In the experiments reported, QUBO produced a slightly better average objective value (average feasible‑solution performance) compared with penalty dephasing and Zeno under the chosen parameters, and showed a different feasibility‑vs‑optimality tradeoff (more constrained landscape).

[speculative] The authors attribute QUBO's higher iteration count and longer optimization time to a more rugged/complex optimization landscape caused by embedded penalty terms (more local minima / potential barren‑plateau effects).

[speculative] The authors suggest Zeno's suboptimal performance in their experiments may stem from the absence of post‑selection and the practical overhead of frequent mid‑circuit measurements, which they note increase simulation complexity.

[speculative] The paper proposes that the quantum Zeno effect can be used in QAOA to confine evolution to the feasible subspace by frequent projections (theoretical proposal / extension of prior Zeno literature).

[supported] Experimental setup details reported: classical simulation of QAOA variants, averaging over 50 random knapsack instances; example parameter settings included p = 5 for many comparisons, QUBO penalty P = 10 and penalty dephasing weight α = 10000.
results_summary: The authors performed classical simulations comparing three constraint‑encoding strategies for QAOA (quadratization/QUBO, penalty dephasing, and a quantum Zeno–based approach) on randomly generated knapsack instances. QUBO used fewer ancilla qubits and two‑qubit gates per layer but required more classical optimizer iterations and longer simulation runtime; it produced slightly better average feasible‑solution quality under the tested parameters. Penalty dephasing improved the probability of finding the best feasible solution with more QAOA layers and showed the best average performance at an intermediate layer count in these experiments. The Zeno approach incurred larger simulation runtime due to mid‑circuit measurements (mixed‑state simulation) and, without post‑selection, delivered suboptimal performance in the tested settings. Resource costs scaled upward with problem size for all methods. The authors conclude that no single encoding is uniformly superior and that choice should be tailored to problem specifics and available resources.
quantum_advantage_detail: The manuscript presents a comparative, classical‑simulation study of three constraint encodings for QAOA; it does not claim or demonstrate any quantum computational advantage over classical algorithms or classical baselines. The results are comparative observations about resource usage and empirical behavior of encodings in simulation rather than demonstrations of quantum speedup or advantage.
limitations: All experiments were conducted using classical simulation on commercial laptops (no experiments on real quantum hardware).
Study limited to small problem sizes (reported results for number of items m in the range ~3–6), limiting conclusions about scalability.
Zeno variant was evaluated without post-selection (authors deliberately excluded post-selection), which may understate its potential performance.
Simulating the Zeno circuits produces mixed states and is substantially more expensive in classical simulation (longer runtimes), complicating evaluation.
[inferred] Penalty parameters were fixed (e.g., P=10 for QUBO, alpha=10000 for penalty dephasing) and parameter sensitivity/robust tuning was not explored.
[inferred] Only a single classical optimizer (COBYLA) was used; the impact of optimizer choice on convergence and results was not studied.
[inferred] No noise or error models were included; the impact of device noise on the three encoding methods was not evaluated.
Quadratization (QUBO) requires fewer ancilla qubits/two-qubit gates but produced a more rugged optimization landscape and required more optimization iterations and longer runtimes.
Penalty dephasing and Zeno require additional quantum operations (adders, constraint testing, mid-circuit measurements) and thus higher ancilla and two-qubit gate counts per layer.
[inferred] The study relied on specific circuit subroutines (e.g., QFT adder) without comparing alternative, potentially less resource-intensive implementations.
[inferred] Only the knapsack problem was used as a case study; generalizability to other CSP classes and real-world financial problem instances was not demonstrated.
[inferred] Layer depths evaluated were modest (p up to 7); the behavior for deeper QAOA circuits (and associated trainability issues like barren plateaus) was not fully characterized.
[inferred] No direct comparisons to classical optimization algorithms or classical baselines were presented, so the practical advantage is not assessed.
[inferred] Theoretical analysis of why different encodings produce the observed optimization landscape differences (e.g., ruggedness, local minima) is limited.

key_ideas: #idea:near-term-feasibility — Simulation results on small 0/1 knapsack instances (m=3-6) characterize resource and performance trade-offs relevant to NISQ-era QAOA deployments.
#idea:hybrid-approach — Classical optimization (COBYLA) is essential; QUBO encoding creates a more complex cost landscape requiring more classical optimizer iterations.
#idea:near-term-feasibility — Penalty dephasing increases probability of finding best feasible solutions with deeper QAOA layers but at higher resource cost per layer.
#limitation:qubit-count — Quadratization/QUBO uses slack and ancilla qubits (c = ceil(log2(W)) + 1), highlighting ancilla overhead that limits scalable instance sizes.
#limitation:data-encoding — QFT-based adders, slack-variable encoding, and explicit TEST/flag circuits introduce substantial gate and ancilla overheads for constraint enforcement.
#limitation:simulation-only — All experiments are classical simulations (mixed-state simulations for measurements); no experiments were run on actual quantum hardware.
#limitation:no-empirical-validation — Mid-circuit measurement/reinitialization (Zeno approach) and its runtime/measurement-error impacts are discussed but not empirically validated on QPUs.
